L0@P0: August 7, 2024
L1@P0: GIC Asset Allocation
L2@P0: At a special meeting to assess market opportunities
L3@P0: and risks, the Global Investment Committee decided to
L4@P0: eliminate its overweight in long-duration US
L5@P0: Treasuries and eliminate its underweight in the S&P
L6@P0: 500 (both cutting and adding 1.5% of the total
L7@P0: portfolio respectively). While we may make future
L8@P0: changes that could either raise or lower our Fixed
L9@P0: Income and Equity allocations, today’s decision
L10@P0: increases our Global Equity overweight to +4.5% and
L11@P0: cuts our Global Fixed Income and cash allocation to
L12@P0: 4.5% underweight (vs +/-3% previously).
L13@P0: We continue to express our equity overweight with
L14@P0: higher quality, profitable growth companies among US
L15@P0: small and mid-caps along with a thematic overweight in
L16@P0: healthcare equipment. We prefer greater sector
L17@P0: diversification than the broad market and have kept a
L18@P0: position in the S&P 500 equal-weight index. At the same
L19@P0: time, the 16% drop in large cap US technology shares
L20@P0: and 23% drop in the Philadelphia Semiconductor index
L21@P0: in recent days has reduced valuation and concentration
L22@P0: risks for US large caps.
L23@P0: Japan shares fell as much as 25% in local currency terms
L24@P0: before bouncing back. We continue to see structural
L25@P0: opportunity for future performance and diversification in
L26@P0: Japan, but our current position is slightly overweight. In
L27@P0: contrast, our underweight in US large caps benefited
L28@P0: from the recent market decline.
L29@P0: The US Treasury market performed well during the very
L30@P0: fast correction of late July/early August. Since the S&P
L31@P0: 500 hit a peak on July 16, long-duration US Treasuries
L32@P0: rallied as much as 5.5% in price, offsetting equity market
L33@P0: declines. With yields back to historic norms, high quality
L34@P0: bonds and stocks moved in opposite directions during
L35@P0: the equity market drop, providing a partial hedge.
L36@P0: While we continue to keep a US Treasury overweight
L37@P0: centered in intermediate duration securities to earn income and offset volatility, long-term US Treasury yields have now fallen to
L38@P0: levels where bonds are no longer undervalued. Long-term US Treasuries embed significant Federal Reserve easing steps in
L39@P0: future years. While bonds prices will fluctuate with economic conditions, if the Fed were not to cut policy rates below 3% on
L40@P0: average in future years, investors would only receive historically average term premia for long-duration bonds. This befits a
L41@P0: neutral allocation in our view.
L42@P0: Our tactical asset allocation aims to outperform benchmarks measured over 12-18 months. We continue to expect near-term
L43@P0: volatility on political and geopolitical issues. US employment data in July also caused recession fears to surge. Preliminary
L44@P0: August and September jobs data tends on average to be even weaker. However, tracking data for US GDP growth continues at
L45@P0: or above our expectations for growth near 2.5% this year with S&P 500 EPS rising 8% for 2024 to new records. Weak profits and
L46@P0: output in 2022/2023 were masked by strong jobs data. We see interestrate-sensitive economic activity and broader industrial
L47@P0: output recovering despite a slowing jobs market.
L48@P0: In short, we believe asset prices – both equities and fixed income – moved more than fundamentals in recent days. With a
L49@P0: longer-term tactical view of markets, we believe the S&P 500’s mild correction improved likely returns for the coming year.
L50@P0: Steven Wieting
L51@P0: Chief Investment Strategist and Chief Economist

L231@P3: Bonds are affected by a number of risks, including fluctuations in interest rates, credit risk and prepayment risk. In general, as prevailing interest
L232@P3: rates rise, fixed income securities prices will fall. Bonds face credit risk if a decline in an issuer’s credit rating, or creditworthiness, causes a bond’s
L233@P3: price to decline. High yield bonds are subject to additional risks such as increased risk of default and greater volatility because of the lower credit
L234@P3: quality of the issues. Finally, bonds can be subject to prepayment risk. When interest rates fall, an issuer may choose to borrow money at a lower
L235@P3: interest rate, while paying off its previously issued bonds. As a consequence, underlying bonds will lose the interest payments from the investment
L236@P3: and will be forced to reinvest in a market where prevailing interest rates are lower than when the initial investment was made.

L268@P3: Additionally, the underlying collateral supporting non-Agency MBS may default on principal and interest payments. In certain cases, this could cause
L269@P3: the income stream of the security to decline and result in loss of principal. Further, an insufficient level of credit support may result in a downgrade
L270@P3: of a mortgage bond's credit rating and lead to a higher probability of principal loss and increased price volatility. Investments in subordinated MBS
L271@P3: involve greater credit risk of default than the senior classes of the same issue. Default risk may be pronounced in cases where the MBS security is
L272@P3: secured by, or evidencing an interest in, a relatively small or less diverse pool of underlying mortgage loans.
